h1: The 7 Best Cordless Lawn Edgers Under $300 for Crisp Borders, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Cordless Lawn Edgers 2026: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 cordless lawn edgers under $300, scored on blade type, battery kit, edging reach and how much trench work each can handle.
summary: The WORX WG163 is the edger to buy if you want one 20V tool that trims and edges, and the WORX WG898 is the pick for a true trenching blade along walks and flower beds. The Garvee 9 inch kit has the biggest battery in the group, the EWORK ships with two batteries for larger yards, and the budget weed eater style unit is an entry-level option for short runs of edging.
intro: Most people shop for a cordless edger as if it were a smaller lawn mower, and that is the first mistake. An edger does one job: it cuts a clean vertical line where grass meets a walk, driveway or bed. How that line gets cut matters more than the voltage on the sticker. A spinning blade that bites into soil behaves very differently from a string head turned on its side.

This ranking sorts seven 20V cordless edgers by cutting method first, then by battery kit and reach. We reviewed spec sheets, listing details and the kinds of owner complaints that show up again and again for tools in this class. Where a listing leaves a number out, we say so rather than fill it in, and we treat every price as a bucket, not a quote.

products.name: WORX 20V 12" 2-in-1 Cordless String Trimmer & Electric Lawn Edger, WG163
products.verdict: One 20V tool that trims the lawn and edges the walks, from a brand with a deep battery ecosystem.
products.description:
The WG163 is WORX's 12 inch cordless string trimmer that converts into a wheeled edger, and it runs on the 20V battery platform WORX uses across a large range of yard tools. That platform detail matters more than it sounds, because a battery you already own, or can borrow from a blower or drill, lowers the real cost of the tool.

It ranks first because a 2-in-1 handles the whole border routine: trim around the mailbox and fence posts, then flip it to edge along the driveway. A pure edger leaves you reaching for a second tool the moment you meet a tree base or a fence line. The compromise is that string-driven edging is not the same as a blade cutting a trench. It gives a neat line on a lawn that is already maintained, but it will not recut a border that has gone wild for a season.

Buy it if you have a small to medium suburban lot and want to own fewer machines. Skip it if your walks are overgrown and you need to renew the edge from scratch each spring.
pros: Trims and edges with one tool
Runs on a widely shared 20V platform
Familiar brand with easy accessory supply
products.idealFor: Homeowners with a small to medium lot who want one tool for border work.
products.skipIf: You need to cut a fresh trench along neglected walks.

products.name: WORX Cordless Lawn Edger, 20V 7" Trencher for Lawn Border Tending, WG898
products.verdict: A compact 7 inch blade edger that actually digs a defined border, not just trims the grass lip.
products.description:
The WG898 is a dedicated wheeled edger with a 7 inch blade, marketed for trenching along lawn borders, and it shares the 20V battery family with the WG163. It is the closest thing in this ranking to a traditional gas-style edger, shrunk down for battery power.

It takes second place because blade edging is the better method for the job. A spinning blade slices a vertical wall of turf, which stays crisp for weeks, while string edging fades faster. Against the WG163 the tradeoff is flexibility: this tool does one thing and cannot trim under a hedge or around a fence. A 7 inch blade also means a smaller diameter than the 9 inch Garvee, so it covers less depth at each pass.

It is the right buy for people with long straight runs of walkway and bed edges who care about the finished line. If your edges are mostly curved garden beds, a smaller wheeled tool can feel awkward to steer around tight bends.
pros: Blade cuts a crisp vertical edge
Compact body is easy to store
products.idealFor: Owners with long straight walks who want a defined trench.
products.skipIf: You want a single tool to trim and edge.

products.name: Garvee 20V 9" Cordless Lawn Edger with 4.0Ah Battery & Charger
products.verdict: A 9 inch edger with a 4.0Ah battery in the box, aimed at people who hate stopping mid-yard.
products.description:
The Garvee pairs a 9 inch blade with a 4.0Ah, 20V battery and charger in one kit. Amp-hours measure how much charge the pack holds, and 4.0Ah is the generous end for a 20V tool, roughly double what budget kits ship with.

It lands third because the battery gives it real staying power, but the brand has a much thinner support record than WORX, and the listing does not spell out the blade material or the depth adjustment range. The larger 9 inch blade should leave a deeper cut than the WG898 in principle, which suits thick turf, though a bigger blade also demands more from the battery on each pass.

Buy it if you have a long perimeter, such as a corner lot with sidewalk on two sides, and value finishing in one session. Think twice if you want a proven service network, because replacement batteries for a lesser known brand can be harder to find in five years.
pros: Charger bundled, nothing extra to buy
Strong value for the price bucket
products.idealFor: Corner lots and long perimeters that need one big battery.
products.skipIf: You want a brand with a long service record.

products.name: EWORK 20V Cordless Lawn Edger with 2 Batteries & Charger for Lawns Care
products.verdict: Ships with two batteries and a charger, so one can charge while you work the other.
products.description:
The EWORK edger is sold as a 20V kit with two batteries and a charger. The listing does not state blade diameter or pack capacity, so the appeal here is the logistics rather than a spec: swap packs, keep working.

It ranks fourth because two packs of unknown size are still an unknown. Two small batteries can total less runtime than the single 4.0Ah pack in the Garvee kit, and without a stated amp-hour figure there is no way to compare them on paper. What you do get is redundancy, which is genuinely handy if one cell dies or if the charger sits in the garage while you work at the far end of the yard.

It suits buyers with a mid-size lot who prefer the swap-and-go routine. Before ordering, check the listing for the amp-hour rating of each pack, since that single number decides whether two batteries beat one.
pros: Two batteries allow swap and go
Backup pack if one cell fails
Suits larger lots with long edges
cons: Blade size missing from the listing
products.idealFor: Mid-size yards where one charge may not finish the job.
products.skipIf: You want published runtime and blade figures.

products.name: VEVOR Lawn Edger 8.8-in Blade, 20V Battery Powered Cordless Edger Lawn Tool
products.verdict: An 8.8 inch blade from a tool-focused brand, without the proven track record of WORX.
products.description:
VEVOR sells this as a 20V edger with an 8.8 inch blade, a diameter that sits between the WORX 7 inch and the Garvee 9 inch. VEVOR is better known for workshop and commercial equipment, so the brand is at least accustomed to selling tools, though yard care is not its core.

It ranks fifth because the blade size is attractive but the listing is light on the battery details that decide how long you can actually edge. Whether a battery and charger come with the tool is something to confirm before buying, since some bare-tool listings in this class omit them. If you already own compatible 20V packs, that changes the math in its favor.

Buy it if you want a large blade at a modest price and are comfortable reading the listing carefully. Skip it if you need guaranteed accessory availability or a long warranty process.
products.idealFor: Buyers wanting a larger blade without paying brand premiums.
products.skipIf: You want a clearly listed battery and charger.

products.name: Cordless Lawn Edger, 20V Battery Powered Edger for Lawns Sidewalk
products.verdict: A no-name 20V sidewalk edger that sells a battery kit and little else on paper.
products.description:
This generic listing describes a 20V battery edger for lawns and sidewalks, sold with a battery kit, and gives almost nothing in the way of blade size, weight or runtime. That is typical of marketplace brands, and it is the main reason it sits this low.

It does the same fundamental job as the others, and for light annual touch-ups along a short walk the difference between a well known and unknown edger is small. The real risk is practical: if a blade wears or a battery fails, an unbranded tool offers few good paths to a replacement part, so the purchase is closer to disposable.

It makes sense for a tiny yard or occasional use, where the edger will see a few hours a year. Anyone planning weekly use should step up to a brand with documented parts.
pros: Battery kit listed with the tool
products.idealFor: Small yards where edging happens a few times a year.
products.skipIf: You edge weekly or want parts support.

products.name: 20V Electric Weed Wacker Edger Lawn Tool, Battery Powered Weed Eater 12-Inch Cordless String Trimmer Grass Trimmer Lightweight Yard Tools...
products.verdict: The cheapest way to get a trimmer that can also edge, with a 2.0Ah battery and charger.
products.description:
This is a 12 inch, 20V string trimmer that doubles as an edger, bundled with a 2.0Ah battery and charger. It sits in the lowest price bucket here, under $50, and it is essentially a budget copy of the 2-in-1 idea behind our top pick.

It ranks last because a 2.0Ah pack is the smallest capacity in the group, and a 12 inch string swath chews through battery on thick growth. It will keep a tidy yard tidy, but it is not the tool for heavy grass or long runs. Treat it as a lightweight helper, and expect to recharge before you reach the end of a large property.

It is a sensible buy for townhouse lawns, patios and short walks. If your edging jobs are longer than a quarter of an hour, the larger batteries higher in this ranking are worth the extra spend.
pros: Lowest price bucket in the ranking
products.idealFor: Townhouse lawns and short walks on a tight budget.
products.skipIf: Your yard needs more than one battery charge.

whatMatters.detail: A blade edger spins a metal blade vertically and slices a wall of turf, which stays sharp-looking for weeks. A string trimmer turned on its side clips the grass lip, which looks clean for days and then blurs. For a first-time cut along a neglected walk, a blade wins. To check a listing, look for the word blade and a stated diameter, not just the word edger.

Voltage tells you the power class of the platform, and amp-hours tell you how long the pack lasts. Two 20V tools can differ by a factor of two in runtime if one ships with a 4.0Ah pack and the other with 2.0Ah. Look for the Ah figure in the listing title or specs, and remember that heavy turf drains packs faster than the sticker implies.

If you already own 20V batteries from a drill or blower, buying a bare tool that fits can save real money and keeps your charger count down. The catch is that not every 20V label means the same connector. Confirm that the tool is from the same brand family as your packs, and check whether the listing says tool only or kit.

A bigger blade reaches deeper into soil and takes a thicker bite per pass, but it also asks more of the battery. Blades in this group run from 7 to 9 inches. Check the listing for a depth adjustment control, because the ability to set cut depth is what stops you from scalping a lawn on soft ground.

Wheeled edgers track a straight line along a hard surface far better than handheld ones, and the wheel sets the guide for your cut. Long straight walks reward wheels, while tightly curved beds favor smaller, handheld tools. Look at the listing photos to see where the wheel sits relative to the blade, since that spacing controls how close you can edge to the pavement.

faq.q: Can I use my existing 20V drill battery with these edgers?
faq.a: Only if the edger is from the same brand family as the battery. A 20V label on the box does not guarantee the connectors match, so check the manufacturer's compatibility list. If it does not match, buy a kit with its own battery.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake when buying a cordless edger?
faq.a: Assuming a string trimmer in edging mode will behave like a blade edger. It will clip the lip of the lawn neatly but it will not cut a trench in dirt. If you need a defined border, choose a blade model such as the WORX WG898.

faq.q: Is a cordless edger worth it over a gas one?
faq.a: For a typical suburban lot, yes. A 20V tool is quieter, starts with a button and needs no fuel mixing. Gas models still win for large properties and heavy, compacted soil, where a small battery would run out quickly.

faq.q: How do I set up a wheeled edger for the first time?
faq.a: Charge the battery fully, attach the guard, and set the depth to its shallowest setting. Make a test pass along a hidden section of the lawn and lower the blade a notch at a time until the cut looks right. Starting shallow avoids scalping the turf.

faq.q: How do I maintain the blade and battery?
faq.a: Brush off soil and grass after each use and check the blade for chips or dull spots. Store the battery indoors at room temperature, since cold garages shorten pack life, and top it off before long storage.
It is best avoided. Wet turf clumps, clogs the guard and makes the blade or string work harder, which drains the battery faster. Wait for the lawn to dry and you will get a cleaner line.

finalTake: The WORX WG163 is the best all-round cordless edger in this price range because it trims and edges from one 20V tool. If the border line matters most, the WORX WG898 cuts a real trench. The Garvee 9 inch kit is the value pick for long perimeters, and the EWORK offers two batteries for bigger yards. Check the amp-hour figure and blade size on any listing before you buy, since those two numbers decide how the tool will feel on a Saturday morning.
